To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Ca2+ inward and the slow K+ outward currents are voltage‐dependent and that the slow K+ current is Ca2+‐dependent.
the Ca2+ inward and the Ca2+-activated K+ outward currents are voltage-dependent and time-dependent, the former being activated by depolarization and inactivated at more positive potentials.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the properties of the calcium inward current and the activation and properties of a slow potassium current in voltage‐clamed mouse neuroblastoma.
the study of calcium currents (ICa) in neuroblastoma cells in culture.
the study of the ionic mechanisms of excitation in the nervous system and with the role of calcium ions in the generation of electrical activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IK(Ca), in the mouse neuroblastoma N1E‐155, is activated by Ca2+ entry through ICa, but the mechanism of activation remains to be elucidated.
Ca2+ is a key factor in the control of the membrane potential of the N1E‐15 cell.
IK(Ca), as recorded here, depends on both Ca2+ influx and membrane potential.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the voltage‐dependent inactivation of ICa and the activation of the slow K+ current are independent of each other and are not coupled in any direct way.
Ca2+ influx is a prerequisite for the activation of a Ca2+‐activated K+ current in N1E‐ 115 cells.
Ca2+ influx through ICa activates a K+ conductance, which in turn hyperpolarizes the membrane and reduces the Ca2+ influx.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have shown that the Ca2+ channel and the Ca2+-dependent K+ channel are not only functionally linked, but that they are also physically linked, and that the Ca2+-binding protein, calmodulin, plays an important role in this link.
we have developed an in vitro model system to study the molecular and cellular mechanisms of calcium signaling.
we have developed a method to measure Ca2+ influx into cells using Ca2+‐activated K+ current (IKA).
